title: Data and notebooks
summary: NumPy arrays, aggregates, cleaning CSV data and reproducible runs.

lessons.title: NumPy arrays
lessons.body:
# NumPy arrays

A NumPy array is a block of same-typed numbers. Operations apply to every element, in compiled code, without a Python loop.

```python
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(a * 10)     # [10 20 30 40]
print(a.dtype, a.shape)  # int64 (4,)
print(a[a > 2])   # [3 4]

m = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(m[1, 2])    # row 1, column 2
print(m[:, 0])    # first column
```

`a > 2` produces an array of booleans, known as a mask. Using it as an index keeps the matching elements.

## Views and copies

A slice is a view, not a copy. Changing it changes the original.

```python
b = a[:2]
b[0] = 99
print(a[0])  # 99
c = a.copy()  # independent
```

A mask index, unlike a slice, always returns a new array.
lessons.task: Write `grid(rows, cols)` returning an int array of the numbers from 0 in that shape. Write `last_column(matrix)` returning the final column. Write `above_mean(values)` returning the elements strictly above the mean. Write `zero_negatives(values)` returning a copy with negatives set to 0, leaving the input unchanged.

checks.name: grid has the right shape and values
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = grid(2, 3)
assert got.shape == (2, 3), got.shape
assert np.array_equal(got, [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]), got
assert grid(1, 1).shape == (1, 1), grid(1, 1).shape

checks.name: last column
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = last_column(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]))
assert np.array_equal(got, [2, 4, 6]), got

checks.name: above the mean
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = above_mean(np.array([1, 2, 3, 10]))
assert np.array_equal(got, [10]), got

checks.name: equal values are not above the mean
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = above_mean(np.array([5, 5, 5]))
assert got.size == 0, got

checks.name: zeroes negatives
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = zero_negatives(np.array([-1, 2, -3, 0]))
assert np.array_equal(got, [0, 2, 0, 0]), got

checks.name: input is unchanged
checks.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.array([-1, 2])
zero_negatives(values)
assert np.array_equal(values, [-1, 2]), values

hints: `reshape` turns a flat array into rows and columns. `matrix[:, k]` means every row, column `k`.
`values.mean()` gives a single number. Comparing an array to a number produces a mask you can index with.
`values[values > values.mean()]`, and for the last one: `result = values.copy()`, then `result[result < 0] = 0`.
lessons.explanation:
Masks replace the loop-and-if pattern with one expression, and the work runs in compiled code. Each operation is `O(n)`, with a much smaller constant than a Python loop.

Assigning through a mask writes into the array you index, so `values[values < 0] = 0` would have changed the caller's data. The explicit `.copy()` prevents that.

lessons.title: Broadcasting and aggregates
lessons.body:
# Broadcasting and aggregates

Aggregates such as `sum`, `mean`, `max` and `argmax` collapse an array. The `axis` argument picks the direction that disappears.

```python
import numpy as np

m = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 4.]])
print(m.sum())        # 10.0
print(m.sum(axis=0))  # columns: [4. 6.]
print(m.sum(axis=1))  # rows: [3. 7.]
```

## Broadcasting

Operations between different shapes work when, reading from the last dimension, each pair of sizes is equal or one of them is 1. The size-1 side is stretched.

```python
print(m - m.mean(axis=0))
print(m.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
```

`m.mean(axis=0)` has shape `(2,)`, which lines up with columns, so each column has its own mean subtracted.

To work per row, you need shape `(2, 1)`. `keepdims=True` keeps the collapsed axis as size 1, so the result broadcasts against rows correctly.
lessons.task: Write `center_columns(m)` subtracting each column's mean from that column. Write `row_shares(m)` dividing each row by its own sum, leaving all-zero rows as zeros. Write `best_column(m)` returning the index of the column with the largest total, as an int.

checks.name: centers each column
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = center_columns(np.array([[1.0, 10.0], [3.0, 30.0]]))
assert np.allclose(got, [[-1, -10], [1, 10]]), got
assert np.allclose(got.mean(axis=0), 0), got

checks.name: row shares sum to one
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = row_shares(np.array([[1, 3], [2, 2]]))
assert np.allclose(got, [[0.25, 0.75], [0.5, 0.5]]), got

checks.name: zero rows stay zero
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = row_shares(np.array([[0, 0], [1, 1]]))
assert np.allclose(got, [[0, 0], [0.5, 0.5]]), got
assert not np.isnan(got).any(), got

checks.name: input is not changed
checks.code:
import numpy as np
m = np.array([[1.0, 3.0]])
row_shares(m)
center_columns(m)
assert np.array_equal(m, [[1.0, 3.0]]), m

checks.name: best column
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = best_column(np.array([[1, 9, 2], [3, 1, 2]]))
assert got == 1, got
assert type(got) is int, type(got)
assert best_column(np.array([[5, 5]])) == 0, "first wins a tie"

hints: Decide which direction collapses: `axis=0` gives one value per column, and `axis=1` gives one per row.
Dividing by per-row totals needs shape `(rows, 1)`, so use `keepdims=True`. `np.divide` has `out` and `where` arguments for skipping a division.
`totals = m.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)`, then `np.divide(m, totals, out=np.zeros_like(m, dtype=float), where=totals != 0)`. And `int(m.sum(axis=0).argmax())`.
lessons.explanation:
Broadcasting compares shapes from the right, so `(n, k)` with `(k,)` matches columns while `(n, k)` with `(n, 1)` matches rows. That is the whole purpose of `keepdims`.

`where` skips division at positions where it is false, and those positions keep the value from `out`, which is why zero rows stay zero and no warning appears.

lessons.title: CSV and cleaning data
lessons.body:
# CSV and cleaning data

Real CSV files contain stray spaces, blanks and duplicates. Use the `csv` module rather than `split(",")`, because quoted fields may contain commas.

```python
import csv, io

text = 'name,city\n"Doe, Jo",Oslo\n'
reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text))
for row in reader:
    print(row["name"])  # Doe, Jo
```

`DictReader` uses the header row as keys. Every value is a string, and a row with too few fields gets `None` for the missing ones. For a file, pass an open file with `newline=""` instead of `StringIO`.

## A cleaning routine

- Trim whitespace before anything else.
- Convert types, deciding what to do with failures.
- Choose a rule for duplicates, and normalize before comparing.
- Keep the rules in one function, so you can read and rerun them.

In a notebook, keep the original data untouched and clean into a new variable. Then you can compare the two and rerun from the top.
lessons.task: Write `clean_rows(text)` reading CSV text with `name` and `age` columns and returning a list of `{"name": str, "age": int}`. Trim both fields, drop rows with an empty name or an age that is not a whole number, and drop later duplicates of a name, ignoring case. Write `average_age(rows)` returning the mean, or `None` if there are no rows.

checks.name: reads and trims
checks.code:
got = clean_rows("name,age
  Ada , 36 
Alan,41
")
assert got == [{"name": "Ada", "age": 36}, {"name": "Alan", "age": 41}], got

checks.name: handles quoted commas
checks.code:
got = clean_rows('name,age\n"Doe, Jo",30\n')
assert got == [{"name": "Doe, Jo", "age": 30}], got

checks.name: drops bad rows
checks.code:
text = "name,age
Ada,abc
,20
Bo,
Cy
Di,4.5
Ed,7
"
got = clean_rows(text)
assert got == [{"name": "Ed", "age": 7}], got

checks.name: drops later duplicates, ignoring case
checks.code:
got = clean_rows("name,age
Ada,1
ADA,2
 ada ,3
")
assert got == [{"name": "Ada", "age": 1}], got

checks.name: a bad first row does not block a good second
checks.code:
got = clean_rows("name,age
Ada,x
Ada,5
")
assert got == [{"name": "Ada", "age": 5}], got

checks.name: average age
checks.code:
assert average_age([{"name": "a", "age": 2}, {"name": "b", "age": 4}]) == 3, "mean of 2 and 4"
assert average_age([]) is None, average_age([])
assert clean_rows("name,age\n") == [], clean_rows("name,age\n")

hints: `csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text))` takes care of quoting and headers. A short row gives `None`, not an empty string.
Clean in stages for each row: trim, validate the name, convert the age, then record the name as seen. Only a kept row should count as seen.
`(row.get("age") or "").strip()` handles `None`. Use `try: age = int(age)`, `except ValueError: continue`, and a `seen` set of `name.lower()`.
lessons.explanation:
Recording a name as seen only after the row passes validation means a broken row cannot block a good one with the same name. That detail often goes unnoticed until it hides data.

The set makes the duplicate check `O(1)`, so the whole clean is `O(n)`. `int("4.5")` raises `ValueError`, so fractional ages are rejected rather than silently truncated.

lessons.title: Reproducibility with seeds
lessons.body:
# Reproducibility with seeds

Pseudo-random numbers come from a generator that starts at a seed. The same seed gives the same sequence, so a run can be repeated exactly.

```python
import random

a = random.Random(42)
b = random.Random(42)
print(a.random() == b.random())  # True
```

## Own your generator

`random.seed(42)` sets one shared global generator. Any other code calling `random.random()` will shift your sequence, and your code will shift theirs. Creating `random.Random(seed)` keeps the stream private.

NumPy has the same idea: `np.random.default_rng(seed)`.

## Notebooks

Notebook cells can run in any order, and that is a common reason for results that cannot be reproduced. Before you trust a result, restart and run every cell from the top.

## Limits

A seed reproduces a sequence for a given version of the library. Do not hard-code expected random values across Python versions. Save the seed and the results together.
lessons.task: Write `shuffled_copy(items, seed)` returning a new list shuffled by `random.Random(seed).shuffle`. Write `split_rows(rows, test_fraction, seed)` shuffling a copy the same way and returning `(train, test)`, where `test` is the first `int(len(rows) * test_fraction)` shuffled rows. Neither may change the input or the global generator.
lessons.starter:
import random


def shuffled_copy(items, seed):
    random.seed(seed)
    random.shuffle(items)
    return items


def split_rows(rows, test_fraction, seed):
    return rows, []
lessons.solution:
import random


def shuffled_copy(items, seed):
    result = list(items)
    random.Random(seed).shuffle(result)
    return result


def split_rows(rows, test_fraction, seed):
    shuffled = shuffled_copy(rows, seed)
    count = int(len(rows) * test_fraction)
    return shuffled[count:], shuffled[:count]

checks.name: uses the seeded shuffle
checks.code:
import random
items = list(range(20))
want = list(items)
random.Random(7).shuffle(want)
assert shuffled_copy(items, 7) == want, shuffled_copy(items, 7)

checks.name: same seed, same result
checks.code:
items = list(range(50))
assert shuffled_copy(items, 1) == shuffled_copy(items, 1), "should repeat"
assert shuffled_copy(items, 1) != shuffled_copy(items, 2), "different seeds should differ"

checks.name: input is unchanged
checks.code:
items = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
shuffled_copy(items, 3)
split_rows(items, 0.4, 3)
assert items == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], items

checks.name: global generator is untouched
checks.code:
import random
random.seed(123)
want = random.random()
random.seed(123)
shuffled_copy([1, 2, 3], 9)
split_rows([1, 2, 3], 0.5, 9)
got = random.random()
assert got == want, "use random.Random(seed), not random.seed"

checks.name: split matches the shuffled order
checks.code:
import random
rows = list(range(10))
order = list(rows)
random.Random(5).shuffle(order)
train, test = split_rows(rows, 0.3, 5)
assert test == order[:3], test
assert train == order[3:], train

checks.name: split sizes at the edges
checks.code:
train, test = split_rows([1, 2, 3], 0.0, 1)
assert (len(train), test) == (3, []), (train, test)
train, test = split_rows([1, 2, 3], 1.0, 1)
assert (train, len(test)) == ([], 3), (train, test)
assert split_rows([], 0.5, 1) == ([], []), split_rows([], 0.5, 1)

hints: `list(items)` makes the copy. Then build a private generator with `random.Random(seed)`, instead of touching the global one.
Reuse `shuffled_copy` inside `split_rows`, then slice at the count. Watch which slice is `test` and which is `train`.
`random.Random(seed).shuffle(result)`, then `count = int(len(rows) * test_fraction)` and `return shuffled[count:], shuffled[:count]`.
lessons.explanation:
A private `Random` object has no effect on code that uses the module-level functions, and they have no effect on it, so calling order elsewhere cannot change your split. The shuffle is `O(n)`.

The checks compute their expected values with the same seeded generator rather than storing numbers, so they stay valid even if a future Python version changes the shuffle algorithm.
